8a294314bf50: What did early A.A. take from the Oxford Group, and why did it separate?
07157bfa771d: Both co-founders got their start in the Oxford Group, a Christian movement of the 1930s. Bill W. came to it through his friend Ebby in late 1934; Dr. Bob had been going to its meetings in Akron for about two and a half years.
51d8ad03ba2d: From it early A.A. took the practices of self-examination, admitting defects to another person, making restitution, and giving of oneself to others, along with prayer and dependence on God. Bill said these came "straight from the Oxford Groups" and from its American leader, the Rev. Sam Shoemaker.
66a510757503: The alcoholics left because some Oxford Group ways did not work with drunks: pressure and aggressive evangelism, "team guidance," the "absolutes" as a dose too strong at first, and an emphasis on prominent names that clashed with the alcoholics' wish to stay anonymous. The Oxford Group also aimed to change the whole world, while the alcoholics kept to alcoholics.
c2deb9508cd6: New York separated in 1937. Cleveland's members broke away in May 1939, and Akron's late in 1939. The 1939 Big Book never names the Oxford Group.
1b7848bf989c: <0>Dr. Bob, 1948</0> (his last major talk, printed in P-53). Both men had been associated with the Oxford Group, "Bill in New York, for five months, and I in Akron, for two and a half years" (P-53). The group had told Dr. Bob to attend meetings, join a church and pray, and he did, but kept getting drunk (P-53). "Bill had acquired their idea of service. I had not" (P-53). The one thing they hadn't told him was what Bill did that first Sunday: "attempt to be helpful to somebody else." (P-53). He also said the Oxford Group's Four Absolutes were "the only yardsticks we had in the early days, before the Steps" (P-53). See <1>What were the "Four Absolutes"? Are they in the Big Book?</1>
42dde74eb188: What A.A. took (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)
16cf0ef7a60e: At the 1955 convention Bill said the early A.A. got "its ideas of self-examination, acknowledgment of character defects, restitution for harm done, and working with others straight from the Oxford Groups and directly from Sam Shoemaker" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), "and from nowhere else." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He adds that some Oxford Group attitudes had proved unsuited to A.A.'s purpose, and that Shoemaker's own views on those had later changed (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In the same book, Bill names three sources of the word-of-mouth program: the Oxford Groups, William James and Dr. Silkworth (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
5c4933f4af57: Why they separated (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)
d9dcd9879c7a: "Our debt to them, nevertheless, was and is immense, and so the final breakaway was very painful." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In Akron, he says, the members withdrew "later, and well after the A.A. book was published" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
edd4c79e9c9a: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (1980)</0> describes the Oxford Group as a movement founded by Frank Buchman, a Lutheran minister, which sought to recapture first-century Christianity through surrender to God, self-examination, confession, restitution and giving without reward (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). It says many Oxford Groupers were disappointed in the Big Book because it didn't mention the group and the Twelve Steps had replaced the absolutes (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). It gives the reasons offered for leaving the group unnamed: A.A. had to avoid looking affiliated with any religious group, Catholics were coming in, and, a reason it says "never came out publicly," Buchman was regarded by some as sympathetic to Hitler after a widely publicized interview in 1936 (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). After the Cleveland members left in May 1939 (see <1>How did the Cleveland group become the first to call itself Alcoholics Anonymous?</1>), the Akron alcoholics moved their meeting to Dr. Bob's house late that year, and on January 2, 1940, he wrote to Bill: "Have definitely shaken off the shackles of the Oxford Group" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).
d813309a553c: <0>Pass It On (1984)</0> says the Oxford Group leaders in New York resented Bill's separate meetings for alcoholics, and that Bill left in 1937 (Pass It On, 1984). It quotes his 1940 letter: "some of the Oxford Group presentation and emphasis upon the Christian message saved my life" (Pass It On, 1984), yet "other attitudes of the O.G. nearly got me drunk again" (Pass It On, 1984). He listed aggressive evangelism, personal publicity, the word "absolute," coercion and "checking," and too little emphasis on tolerance (Pass It On, 1984). 0ec064f36fea: What is the Right of Appeal, and why does the minority matter?
b5459f0fb19e: It has two parts. A minority that thinks the majority is badly wrong is encouraged to file a minority report, and on a grave issue has a duty to take it to the General Service Conference. And anyone working in the structure, paid or unpaid, may petition the General Service Board over a personal grievance "without prejudice or fear of reprisal" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).
9921af8a4655: Why: minorities are often right, and even when they're wrong they force a real debate. "The well-heard minority, therefore, is our chief protection against an uninformed, misinformed, hasty or angry majority" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).
3a451ac99a5e: A related idea is older than the Concepts. In 1946, writing about who should pay for clubs, Bill said that "the majority ought not to try to coerce the minority" (P-17, Money, 1946).
c0ecb6382310: Bill's 1946 essay on money applies it to a disagreement. Most members liked clubs, but not all, so club support should come from those who wanted them: "But the majority ought not to try to coerce the minority into supporting clubs they do not want or need" (P-17, Money, 1946).
bdb928cf0aa3: His 1947 essay on government lists among A.A.'s freedoms "no one set in personal authority over anyone else" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947).
2065005e0c34: The 1955 Conference Charter built minority protection into elections: delegates are chosen "by a two-thirds written ballot or by lot" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955).
6b4bbef97bf1: <0>Appeal.</0> All minorities, "whether in our staffs, committees, corporate boards or among the Trustees," should be encouraged to file minority reports when they think the majority is in considerable error (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). Where a wrong decision could seriously affect A.A. as a whole, the minority should treat presenting a report to the Conference as an actual duty.
de423c61d9b1: <0>Why minorities matter.</0> "In granting this traditional ‘Right of Appeal,’ we recognize that minorities frequently can be right" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). Even when partly or wholly wrong, they compel a thorough debate.

e7e55b5b6061: The diagnosis leads straight to a remedy. "Above everything, we alcoholics must be rid of this selfishness." (p. 62) "We must, or it kills us!" (p. 62) "God makes that possible." (p. 62)

Right after the a, b, c, the book asks what turning our will and our life over to God means, and starts with self-will: "The first requirement is that we be convinced that any life run on self-will can hardly be a success." (p. 60) Living that way, "we are almost always in collision with something or somebody, even though our motives are good" (p. 60).
dbaa74b75ae7: The book draws a picture. Each person is "like an actor who wants to run the whole show" (p. 60), arranging the lights, the scenery and the other players his own way. If only people would do as he wished, the show would be great (p. 61). He may be quite virtuous while he does it, or he may be mean and dishonest, or most likely a mix (p. 61). The show goes badly, he tries harder, he gets angry and self-pitying, and he blames others (p. 61).
215871ed2135: Then the questions. "Is he not really a self-seeker even when trying to be kind?" (p. 61) "Is he not, even in his best moments, a producer of confusion rather than harmony?" (p. 61) The book lines up the retired businessman, the minister, politicians and reformers, the safe-cracker and the alcoholic who is locked up, and asks: "are not most of us concerned with ourselves, our resentments, or our self-pity?" (p. 62)

087e606ad70f: "So our troubles, we think, are basically of our own making." (p. 62) The alcoholic is "an extreme example of self-will run riot, though he usually doesn't think so" (p. 62).
